title: Florence, 1439
hookLine: East and West sign a reunion that doesn't last

cards: "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad." That's a line from the Psalms.
It's also how a decree begins, read aloud in the cathedral of Florence, in Latin and in Greek, with the Eastern emperor present and bishops of East and West in the same church.
Its first Latin words, laetentur caeli, became its name. After the schism and the sack of Constantinople, East and West had signed their names to being one Church again.
Today's word is Florence, and the story of how close they came.

teach.b: First, the long talks. The Greeks came west, emperor and bishops together, partly because their city was in danger and they hoped for help. But they didn't come only for help.

Theologians argued in earnest over the old questions: how the Holy Spirit proceeds, what happens to souls after death, the authority of the pope, even whether the bread of the Mass should be leavened or unleavened.
The decree tried to show that the two sides often meant the same truth in different words. On the bread, it said both customs were valid: the Latins could keep theirs and the Greeks theirs.
It's a careful, generous document. Next, the one who wouldn't sign.
Mark, the bishop of Ephesus, refused; he was sure the agreement gave away too much. Orthodox Christians honor him as a saint for standing firm.
Catholics remember the council as a real reunion that was not received. Finally, the homecoming. When the delegates went back east, clergy and people refused what had been signed.
The union never took hold, and after a while it was set aside.
On paper they were one. In the parishes, they were not. Still, it isn't a story of failure only.
Florence showed that East and West could sit at one table, pray in one church, and find shared words, which is worth remembering whenever the two churches talk today.

how: Catholic and Orthodox churches continue formal theological dialogue today, and their leaders meet and pray together; the Council of Florence is remembered by Catholics as a reunion that was signed but not received in the East.

games.q: you're a Greek delegate home from Florence. the decree is signed, but your parish won't accept it. what happens?
o: the parish accepts it because it was signed.
the union never takes hold and is set aside.
the emperor forces everyone to agree.
games.why: clergy and people in the East would not receive the union, and it never took hold: almost one.

practice: Bring to mind a reconciliation you've tried, maybe more than once, that didn't hold, with a friend, a sibling, a parent, an old colleague, and instead of replaying the fight, notice what you did agree on, even if it was small.
Then picture the smallest next step that wouldn't cost your honesty: a message, a kind word, a door left open. If you pray, pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Florence. The council where East and West signed a decree of reunion that began, let the heavens rejoice, and that the East did not receive. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: let the heavens rejoice — the opening words, and so the name, of the Florence decree of union.

carryVoice: Your line: almost one. A stalled peace isn't a finished one. That's day seven hundred eighty.
